✅ Approved the contribution.
Comment: Great data rep, loved the intervals. Great job.

Hi, 

Can't find the same results than you in Fat Squares, Fat Squares Validator, Black Hole, Black Hole Validator. For the others, my solution agreed with your output.

I have a big doubt about the Fat Squares Validator output : 
Tile 602 902 : Square 1 and 4  => Area         25
Tile 980     2 : Square 3             => Area   10000
Tile 960 555 : Square 2             => Area   20000
Tile 111 222 : Square 1             => Area 789975
Tile 888 666 : Square 1 and 2  => Area   20000
Tile 907 300 : No square          => Area   40000 according to the output / 160000 according to me
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Total                                                  Area  88000                                             1000000

I think there is no other area in the grid so the sum should be side * side, but I might be wrong.

Could you please have a look ? 
Thanks a lot ;)

✅ Approved the contribution.
Comment: Tricky puzzle involving good data representation and interval handling. Very instructive!

[Goal]

- For clarity, consider adding "distinct bounded non-overlapping regions" to the end of the first sentence.

- Please correct "triple" to "triplet".

- For clarity, consider adding to the second sentence "coordinates of the top-left-most tile contained within its boundaries".

- For clarity, consider changing "Tile X (x, y): Region area = A" to "The region containing tile X (x, y) has an area of A."

[Input/Constraints/Stub]

- Please differentiate between the coordinates of the squares (e.g., ([[sx]], [[sy]])) and the coordinates of the target tiles (e.g. ([[tx]], [[ty]])).

[Output]

- Please rephrase "area of the region for the corresponding target tile" to "area of the region containing the corresponding target tile".

[Cases]

- I notice that the tests/validators feature a large number of coordinates near the top left of the bounded grid, and a handful more at the other corners. Only the "Fat Squares" test/validator tests a wide range of coordinates. Without a wider range of coordinates, players might be tempted to employ brute force methods on a set of much smaller grids (e.g. monitoring the four corners of the large grid). Please rework/add some tests/validators to vary the coordinate range according to the grid size.

Thank you :)

Output
* Please format "[[N]] lines" in <<bold>>.

Constraints
* Please add:
1 ≤ [[x]], [[y]], [[s]] ≤ [[side]]

Stub generator
* Please replace Lines 2 and 3 with:
loop M read x:int y:int s:int
loop N read x:int y:int

Tags
* Consider removing "Set theory" and "Coarse granularity".

* Consider adding "Coordinates". (Your puzzle reminds me of another puzzle, Cloudy Weather: https://www.codingame.com/training/hard/cloudy-weather .)

Solution
* I didn't study your solution in detail, but I noticed that the `addSquare` method reads each square in the order of y, x, s instead of x, y, s. Does this affect the correctness of the expected outputs?

Cases
* Dartboard (Validator 6) appears to be the only case where two squares touch along one side. Please revise Test 6 to include the same situation.

Thanks.

Thanks your review and comments. All adopted.

The addSquare() method is now updated to x, y, s order together with another method handling x and y also updated to the proper order. It does not affect the correctness of the outputs.

Validator 6 becomes Test 6. A new Validator is created.
Thanks your comments. It will take some time to implement them.
Both "triple" and "triplet" seem to be correct: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuple#Etymology

Hm, guess that was quite a nitpicky comment then. My apologies!

@java_coffee_cup, let me know when you've revised the cases and I'll approve the puzzle :)

The revision is done.

Some of the test and validator cases are updated to include more varied testing locations.
Most of the suggested wordings are adopted. 

The suggestions regarding more precise definitions in the first two sentences were carefully considered. While adding further qualifying adjectives could improve the precision of the statements, it would also make the sentences too dense for a non-specialist audience to follow easily. It was determined that the lack of additional definitions is already adequately compensated for by the illustrative diagram, the worked example, and the statements in the Constraints section.
Looks good to me. Thank you for the quick update.
